sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Geometric Relative Positional Encoding has become the primary mechanism for injecting spatial inductive biases into multi-view transformers. Existing designs condition attention on camera-level frustums or ray-marched depth, associating cross-view tokens through the sensor geometry. Such sensor-centric formulations, however, describe only where a token is observed from, leaving the rich surface geometry of the scene region depicted by the token. In this paper, we advocate a shift toward surface-aware positional encoding that explicitly grounds patch tokens in the geometry of physical surfaces. We introduce HRoPE, which represents the local geometry of each patch as a slanted 3D plane, following the slanted support-window assumption of classical multi-view stereo. We inject token-level, plane-induced homographies into attention as relative transformations. This equips the transformer with a geometric prior for rectifying perspective distortions and aligning patch features across viewpoints. Our encoding requires no ground-truth geometry: the plane parameters can be predicted end-to-end under a view-synthesis objective alone, or derived from foundation models. Extensive experiments on RealEstate10K, CO3Dv2, and DL3DV show that our best variant of HRoPE consistently outperforms the evaluated geometric positional encodings for novel view synthesis. Extensive ablations and analysis show the effectiveness of the proposed encoding. Please refer to our project page at: https://gaohchen.github.io/HRoPE

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: The Transformer has become the de facto architecture for recent feed-forward 3D vision (Wang et al., 2024; 2025; Jin et al., 2025). By tokenizing images from multiple viewpoints and exchanging information via attention, these models exhibit strong capabilities in jointly resolving appearance, visibility, and scene geometry. Attention, however, is permutation-equivariant: it operates on unordered sets and is inherently agnostic to the camera poses, metric scales, and epipolar constraints that couple multi-view observations. Consequently, geometric priors must be explicitly injected, either by conditioning token representations directly (e.g., via camera tokens (Wang et al., 2025) or ray maps (Jin et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024a)) or by imposing epipolar constraints on attention (He et al., 2020; Charatan et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2024). Positional encoding (PE) introduces geometric structure directly into attention by modulating pairwise token comparisons. While existing PE designs exhibit increasing geometric fidelity by using priors from images, cameras, and rays, they invariably anchor positional information to the sensor. RoPE extensions (Su et al., 2024) encode 2D intra-view offsets, leaving inter-view transformations implicit (Weinzaepfel et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024). GTA (Miyato et al., 2024) and CaPE (Kong et al., 2024) inject relative camera extrinsics to achieve invariance to global rigid motions, while PRoPE (Li et al., 2025) generalizes this to the full projection matrix. Ray-based formulations like RayRoPE (Wu et al., 2026) and URoPE (Xie et al., 2026) integrate depth by localizing patches along viewing rays and These authors contributed equally. Corresponding authors. 1 Preprint Figure 1: From sensor-centric to surface-aware geometric positional encoding. Across this progression, geometry is parameterized via sensorcentric abstractions: an image coordinate, camera frustum, or point of ray termination, leaving the rich local surface structure of the underlying scene unmodeled (see Fig. 1, left and middle). This limitation is fundamental because multi-view matching does not compare isolated points; it compares local neighborhoods whose appearances are related through surface-induced deformations. patch in one view and its corresponding patch in another are connected by warp determined by the underlying surface geometry, and reliable correspondence requires compensating for this warp before comparing visual features. Given the pixel location and camera geometry, depth locates the patch center, while surface orientation additionally determines how its surrounding neighborhood deforms across views. By providing only view or positional information, existing PEs implicitly impose fronto-parallel assumption on the attention computation mechanism. Although large neural models can learn to compensate for this bias given sufficient training data, doing so compromises efficiency and generalization. We argue that surface orientation is the missing degree of freedom: current PEs capture the zeroth-order position of patch but neglect the first-order local orientation that dictates its cross-view appearance transformation. To this end, we present HRoPE, Homography Relative Positional Encoding that embeds orientation-aware rectification directly into the attention mechanism (Fig. 1, right). Inspired by the slanted support windows of classical multi-view stereo (Bleyer et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2021a), HRoPE anchors local tangent plane to each patch token. We use the plane normal and distance, together with the camera poses, to define the homography governing cross-view neighborhood deformations. Concretely, we apply per-patch 3 3 transformation block-diagonally to the queries, keys, and values, and incorporate closed-form inverse into the key projection so that the resulting attention logits depend exclusively on the relative homography between tokens. As we show in Sec. 3.2 and Appendix A.2, this mechanism acts as an in-attention analogue of computing matching score only after both neighborhoods have been rectified onto shared tangent plane. Consequently, whereas prior geometric PEs merely encode where token is located, HRoPE explicitly models how its underlying surface transforms across views. This formulation offers two compelling advantages. First, HRoPE strictly generalizes pointand ray-based PEs: when predicted normal aligns with the viewing direction, the induced transformation naturally reduces to the fronto-parallel case. Second, the per-patch transformation parameters can be regressed from patch features by lightweight head trained jointly with the view-synthesis model, using the view-synthesis objective alone. The head can optionally use pretrained features from DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2024) or VGGT (Wang et al., 2025), without changing the encoding formulation or training objective. 2 Preprint We validate HRoPE on feed-forward novel view synthesis (NVS) across the RealEstate10K (Zhou et al., 2018), CO3Dv2 (Reizenstein et al., 2021), and DL3DV (Ling et al., 2024) datasets, where it consistently outperforms view-, projection-, and ray-based encodings. Notably, HRoPE surpasses PRoPE on RealEstate10K without ground-truth camera poses, demonstrating that per-patch homography is stronger prior than view-level projection. Furthermore, our ablations show that this geometry must condition token interactions multiplicatively, injecting the same information as additive features sharply degrades performance. Finally, HRoPE improves generalization to unseen zooms and wider baselines, supporting its role as geometric inductive bias. Beyond NVS, HRoPE transfers unchanged to multi-view diffusion model and to the visual tokens of spatial reasoning MLLM, improving performance on both tasks (Appendix A.6). We summarize our main contributions as follows: 1. We formulate the principle of surface-aware positional encoding, positioning local 3D surface geometry as the natural anchor for comparing patch neighborhoods across views. 2. We propose HRoPE, per-patch relative encoding that uses plane-induced transforms with closed-form inverses to condition attention logits on relative cross-view homographies. 3. We demonstrate consistent improvements over the evaluated geometric positional encodings on multiple NVS benchmarks and under out-of-distribution view settings. Controlled ablations analyze the roles of transformation structure, local geometry, and feature source, supporting the benefit of the homography inductive bias.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Geometric Positional Encoding. Geometric PEs encode camera or scene geometry in tokens and attention. Absolute variants encode Plucker rays (Sitzmann et al., 2021; Sajjadi et al., 2022; Jin et al., 2025) or 3D positions (Liu et al., 2022), but depend on the chosen world frame. Relative variants extend rotary encodings (Su et al., 2024; Shaw et al., 2018) to camera geometry: GTA (Miyato et al., 2024) and CaPE (Kong et al., 2024) use relative extrinsics, while PRoPE (Li et al., 2025) also includes intrinsics through projection matrices. Recent methods move from viewto token-level geometry: RayRoPE (Wu et al., 2026) predicts per-token depth, RoRE (Griffiths & Dansereau, 2026) rotates features along rays, and URoPE (Xie et al., 2026) projects per-head depth anchors into the query frame, following epipolar attention (He et al., 2020; Suhail et al., 2022). These encodings describe camera relationships and pointor ray-level geometry. HRoPE adds an explicit local-plane parameterization whose orientation, together with distance and camera geometry, determines planar neighborhoods cross-view deformation. This distinguishes surface-conditioned transformations from point localization without requiring the latter to assume fronto-parallel surfaces. Multi-view Transformers. Multi-view transformers use camera geometry to associate image tokens across views. Their applications include stereo depth estimation (He et al., 2020; Yao et al., 2018; Gu et al., 2020), camera and structure recovery (Wang et al., 2024; 2025), cross-view completion and matching (Weinzaepfel et al., 2023), spatial reasoning (Yang et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025), and camera-controlled video and world modeling (Li et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2025), as well as novel view synthesis (NVS). For feed-forward NVS, methods use featureconditioned radiance fields (Yu et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021b; Chen et al., 2021; Trevithick & Yang, 2021; Hong et al., 2024), predict 3D Gaussians (Charatan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024a; Zhang et al., 2024a), or directly regress pixels (Jin et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025). We evaluate HRoPE primarily on novel view synthesis using the LVSM backbone with plane-induced positional encoding. Slanted Support Windows. Traditional local stereo methods assume constant disparity within support window, introducing fronto-parallel bias on slanted surfaces (Bleyer et al., 2011). Building on randomized correspondence search (Barnes et al., 2009), PatchMatch Stereo (Bleyer et al., 2011) addresses this limitation by estimating local disparity plane at each pixel and evaluating matching costs over slanted support windows. More generally, local planar geometry induces homography that relates corresponding image neighborhoods across views (Hartley & Zisserman, 2003). Learned multi-view stereo methods also use differentiable geometric warping to compare features under depth hypotheses (Yao et al., 2018; Gu et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021a). Middle: token-specific transforms modulate the cross-view attention, yielding the relative factor Hi,uH1 j,v in each attention logit (Eq. 4). Right: the transform is repeated block-diagonally over the geometric half of each head, while the remaining dimensions retain the 2D rotary blocks Φx and Φy (Eq. 17). principle of using local surface geometry to guide cross-view matching. It incorporates per-patch, plane-induced transformations into multi-view attention, bringing the geometric intuition of slantedwindow matching into positional encoding.

Then, in Sec. 3.2, we introduce the plane-induced transformation and show how it modulates multiview attention. With consistent camera geometry, the relative transformation exactly maps points on shared physical plane across views. For independently predicted per-patch parameters, the same algebraic form modulates attention without requiring an exact physical correspondence for every token pair. We evaluate HRoPE on novel view synthesis by applying it to the decoderonly LVSM (Jin et al., 2025) architecture. Each model takes two reference views as input and synthesizes target view. Following PRoPE (Li et al., 2025), we train downsized LVSM backbone variants (25M parameters) with different positional encoding methods. We train and evaluate the models separately on CO3Dv2 (Reizenstein et al., 2021), RealEstate10K (Zhou et al., 2018), and Objaverse (Deitke et al., 2023), and report PSNR, SSIM (Wang et al., 2004), and LPIPS (Zhang et al., 2018). To evaluate scaling with the number of reference views, we additionally follow the RayZer (Jiang et al., 2025) protocol and train larger LVSM backbone variant (53M parameters) on DL3DV (Ling et al., 2024). We evaluate the model with 2, 4, and 8 reference views on the held-out DL3DV benchmark. Results. Table 1 shows that the VGGT-based HRoPE outperforms baseline PEs on CO3Dv2, RealEstate10K, and Objaverse. Relative to PRoPE, it gains 0.53, 1.27, and 1.03 dB in PSNR, respectively, with higher SSIM and lower LPIPS. On DL3DV, HRoPE also outperforms PRoPE with 2, 4, and 8 reference views  (Table 2)  . PSNR and SSIM gains are largest with two views, suggesting greater benefits under sparse observations. Qualitative comparisons on RealEstate10K show that HRoPE better preserves object boundaries and fine details  (Fig. 3)  . 4.2 ABLATION STUDIES AND ANALYSIS We investigate the design and behavior of HRoPE from three perspectives. Second, we examine the contribution and quality of local geometry through calibrated-camera comparison, qualitative visualizations, and an oracle geometry experiment (Sec. 4.2.2). We first evaluate robustness to changes in camera intrinsics by varying the target-camera focal length at test time. Specifically, we scale the focal length from 1 to 5 its original value, where 1 corresponds to the standard evaluation setting. As shown in Fig. 6, HRoPE maintains strong performance as the zoom factor increases and achieves the lowest LPIPS across the evaluated focal lengths. In contrast, the calibrated variant degrades more substantially under large zoom factors. Target-view Extrapolation. We next extend the target-view sampling interval by 50% at both ends, allowing target views to fall outside the interval bounded by the two reference views. Fig. 6 shows that HRoPE maintains its advantage over the baseline positional encodings as the target view moves beyond the training sampling regime. Input-view Spacing. We additionally vary the temporal spacing between the two reference frames. We shift the input-frame interval from the training range of [25, 100] to [75, 150] at test time. HRoPE remains robust as the reference views become farther apart and achieves lower LPIPS across the evaluated intervals.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: In this paper, we investigated local surface geometry as prior for positional encoding in multiview transformers. Inspired by the slanted support windows of PatchMatch Stereo, we introduced HRoPE, which uses the structure of plane-induced homographies to parameterize per-patch transformations and modulate attention through their relative composition. The transformation parameters 10 Preprint Figure 6: Out-of-distribution generalization on RealEstate10K. Left pair: PSNR () and LPIPS () as the unseen target-camera zoom factor increases from 1 to 5. Right pair: the PSNRLPIPS trade-off under soft target-view extrapolation and an enlarged baseline between the two input views. are predicted from patch features and learned jointly with the view-synthesis model. Experiments on RealEstate10K, CO3Dv2, Objaverse, and DL3DV demonstrate improved novel view synthesis over the evaluated positional encodings. Ablations support the contribution of the transformation structure, with gains observed for predictors trained from scratch and further improvements from pretrained features. calibrated extension also improves PRoPE by incorporating local planar frames while retaining its camera projections. These findings support local surface geometry as useful inductive bias for multi-view attention. Limitations. HRoPE encourages correct cross-view correspondence through the structure of its rectified matching, but does not guarantee it: because the plane parameters are predicted per patch and per view, the encoding offers no formal guarantee that the same physical surface is encoded identically across views, unlike methods that enforce such uniqueness by construction. In practice the learned planes are cross-view consistent and the calibrated bridge corroborates the underlying geometry, but hard guarantee remains future work. 11 Preprint

We then insert the block-diagonal operator in Eq. 17 into the language models self-attention, applying it only to visual tokens in layers 10 through 2 of the 28-layer backbone (L = 28): the i,u and 1 geometric halves of each heads query and key for token (i, u) are transformed by i,u , respectively, where Hi,u = KiAi,u, while the remaining halves retain the native rotary encoding. In this way, the visual stream of the MLLM is explicitly conditioned on per-patch surface geometry, while text tokens and the temporal ordering of frames are left unchanged, making HRoPE strictly additive augmentation to the pretrained VLM.
